title: Computer vision at a glance
intro: Each chapter in a few visual slides: the mental model, the distinctions the questions turn on, and the concepts to practise next.

chapters.hook: Pixels, filters and transforms — and the silent bugs that live in between.

slides.title: The traps that never raise an error
slides.lede: Most image-pipeline bugs do not crash. The model still runs; accuracy just quietly drops.

head: Trap
What happens
rows: OpenCV loads BGR; most models expect RGB. Channels swap silently.
200 + 100 = 44 in NumPy. cv2.add saturates at 255; plain + wraps.
0–255 input to a model trained on ImageNet-normalised data saturates it.
PIL may rotate the image, cv2 does not: same file, different pixels.
Bilinear resizing of a label mask invents class 1.5.

slides.takeaway: Accurate in the notebook, poor in production with identical weights? It is almost always preprocessing parity. Compare the intermediate tensors of both paths first.

slides.title: Pick the filter by the problem
slides.lede: Each filter is the answer to a specific kind of noise or defect. Questions describe the defect.

rows: Gaussian blur — separable into two 1D passes, blurs edges too

slides.takeaway: Blur radius is relative to image scale. The same kernel in pixels smooths differently at different resolutions.

slides.title: Thresholding and contrast
slides.lede: Separating foreground from background depends on how the lighting behaves across the image.

items.label: Otsu
items.text: An automatic global threshold. Works when the histogram is bimodal.

items.label: Adaptive threshold
items.text: A local threshold per region, for uneven illumination where one global value fails.

items.label: CLAHE
items.text: Local contrast enhancement that limits noise amplification in flat regions.

items.label: HSV
items.text: Threshold on hue for colour under changing light — hue survives brightness changes.

points.t: Luma is roughly 0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B, not a flat average — the eye weights green most.

slides.title: Geometric transforms and resizing
slides.lede: Two transform families with different degrees of freedom, and a resizing choice that depends on direction.

cols.title: Affine
items: Rotation, scale, shear, translation
Parallel lines stay parallel

cols.title: Homography
items: Maps a rectangle to any quadrilateral
Valid only for a planar scene or a purely rotating camera

points.t: Shrinking: INTER_AREA, to avoid aliasing. Enlarging: linear or cubic. Label masks: always nearest-neighbour.
Stretching to a square distorts every object. Pad instead — and undo both scale and padding when mapping boxes back.

chapters.hook: Edges, features and camera geometry — still the right tool in controlled settings.

slides.title: From pixels to matched features
slides.lede: The classical pipeline for finding the same points in two images.

points.t: Hysteresis: the high threshold starts an edge; the low one extends it along connected pixels.
An edge is ambiguous along its own direction. A corner is not — which is why keypoints are corners.

slides.title: RANSAC: fitting through outliers
slides.lede: Feature matches always include gross errors. RANSAC finds the model most of the data agrees with and ignores the rest.

nodes.label: Sample
nodes.sub: A random minimal subset — 4 pairs for a homography

nodes.label: Fit
nodes.sub: Solve the model from just those

nodes.label: Score
nodes.sub: Count matches within tolerance — the inliers

visual.loop: repeat for a fixed number of iterations, then refit on all inliers

slides.takeaway: A homography cannot explain parallax. Two viewpoints of a 3D scene give low inlier counts however long RANSAC runs — the model, not the fit, is wrong.

slides.title: Cameras, calibration and depth
slides.lede: To measure anything in the world, first model how the camera maps the world onto pixels.

items.label: Intrinsics
items.text: Focal length, principal point, skew: the camera-to-pixel mapping.

items.label: Extrinsics
items.text: Where the camera sits and points in the world.

items.label: Radial distortion
items.text: Straight lines bow near the edges. Calibrate and undistort before measuring.

items.label: Rectification
items.text: Aligns stereo epipolar lines with image rows, turning a 2D search into 1D.

items.label: Depth from disparity
items.text: Focal length times baseline over disparity. Far points have tiny disparity, so far depth is imprecise.

slides.title: Where classical methods still win
slides.lede: With controlled lighting, fixed cameras and simple shapes, a classical method can be faster, cheaper and more predictable than a learned one.

items.label: Hough transform
items.text: Edge pixels vote in parameter space for lines or circles. Robust to gaps and partial occlusion.

items.label: Template matching
items.text: Finds a known, fixed appearance. Breaks under changes in scale, rotation or lighting.

items.label: Contour shape descriptors
items.text: Describe silhouettes from a clean segmentation — good on a controlled production line.

chapters.hook: How convolutional networks see, and how to choose and reuse one.

slides.title: Convolution mechanics
slides.lede: A handful of choices decide what a convolutional layer can see and what it costs.

items.label: Weight sharing
items.text: One kernel slides everywhere: few parameters, and translation equivariance for free.

items.label: Receptive field
items.text: The input region that can influence a unit. It compounds with depth.

items.label: stacked small kernels
items.text: Same receptive field as one 5×5, fewer parameters, one more non-linearity.

items.label: Stride 2
items.text: Downsamples while convolving, instead of a separate pooling step.

items.label: Dilation
items.text: Widens the receptive field with no extra parameters and no loss of resolution.

items.label: 1×1 convolution
items.text: Mixes channels at each position — a cheap way to change depth.

slides.title: What each depth learns
slides.lede: Early layers learn features that are useful for almost any image. Later layers become specific to the task.

points.t: The generic early layers carry over to a new task; only the specific top needs to change.
An FPN's top-down path gives every scale both deep semantics and fine resolution.

slides.title: Backbone building blocks
slides.lede: Modern backbones are assembled from a few ideas. Each one solved a specific limit.

head: Idea
What it solves
rows: Very deep stacks become trainable — a direct path for the gradient
Cost: a per-channel spatial filter plus 1×1 mixing (MobileNet)
Replaces flatten-plus-dense; tolerates variable input size
Scale depth, width and resolution together, not one axis (EfficientNet)

slides.takeaway: CNNs are translation-equivariant by construction but not rotation-invariant. Rotation robustness has to come from augmentation or the data.

slides.title: BatchNorm has two modes
slides.lede: A layer that behaves differently in training and in inference, and a classic source of train/serve mismatch.

cols.title: Training
items: Normalises with the current batch's statistics
Updates the running mean and variance

cols.title: Inference
items: Uses the stored running statistics
Forgetting eval() gives batch-dependent outputs

points.t: Batch statistics become noisy. GroupNorm normalises within each example instead.
It does not saturate for positive inputs, so gradients survive depth.

slides.title: Transfer learning: how much to unfreeze
slides.lede: The less data you have and the closer your domain is to the pretraining data, the more of the network you keep frozen.

items.label: Gradual unfreezing
items.sub: Top to bottom, lower learning rates below

items.label: Train from scratch
items.sub: Only with very large or very different data

chapters.hook: Augmentation, losses, schedules and the curves that tell you what went wrong.

slides.title: Augment for the world you deploy in
slides.lede: An augmentation should simulate a variation the model will actually meet. One that cannot occur only teaches it about images it will never see.

items.label: Match the domain
items.text: Vertical flip is wrong for street scenes — gravity fixes orientation — and fine for satellite imagery.

items.label: Transform the labels
items.text: Detection boxes and masks move with the image. Handle boxes cropped away or made degenerate.

items.label: Mixup vs mosaic
items.text: Mixup blends images and label distributions — for classification. Detection uses mosaic, which tiles images spatially.

items.label: Training set only
items.text: Validation is a measuring instrument. Augmenting it changes what you measure.

slides.title: Read the training curves
slides.lede: Training and validation loss together tell you which problem you have. Diagnose before adding capacity or data.

head: Symptom
Diagnosis
rows: Overfitting: stop at the validation minimum; add data, augmentation or regularisation
Both plateau high from the start
Underfitting or a pipeline bug: check labels, normalisation and learning rate before capacity
99% train, 55% validation on a tiny set
Expected memorisation — but also check for leakage across the split

points.t: Weight decay and dropout constrain the model; more and more varied data is usually the strongest regulariser.

slides.title: Losses for imbalanced data
slides.lede: In detection, most candidate locations are easy background. Left alone, they dominate the loss.

cols.title: Cross-entropy
items: Every example weighted equally
Thousands of easy negatives swamp the gradient
Rare hard cases barely register

cols.title: Focal loss
items: Down-weights examples already classified confidently
Hard cases drive learning
Made one-stage detectors competitive (RetinaNet)

points.t: Re-weight or re-sample the rare classes, and always report them separately.
Softens one-hot targets so the model is less over-confident.

slides.title: Keeping optimisation stable
slides.lede: Four settings that stop a training run from diverging or silently learning nothing.

items.label: Warmup
items.text: Ramp the learning rate up so early, noisy gradients cannot destabilise training.

items.label: Loss scaling
items.text: Mixed precision needs it: small FP16 gradients otherwise underflow to zero.

items.label: Gradient clipping
items.text: Caps the gradient norm so one pathological batch cannot wreck the run.

items.label: Batch size and LR
items.text: A larger batch means less gradient noise and fewer steps. Scale the learning rate with it.

slides.title: Throughput and experiment hygiene
slides.lede: Two ways to waste compute: a GPU waiting for data, and results you cannot reproduce or trust.

cols.title: Starved GPU
items: The data pipeline is the bottleneck, not the model
More loader workers, faster decoding, caching
A bigger GPU changes nothing

cols.title: Honest experiments
items: Fixed seeds, versioned data and code
Splits decided once, before training
The test set touched only at the end

chapters.hook: The heaviest topic: how detectors work, how they are scored, and how they fail.

slides.title: Three families of detector
slides.lede: Detectors differ in whether they propose regions first, predict densely in one pass, or predict a set directly.

cols.title: Two-stage
items: Propose regions, then classify and refine
Accurate, slower
Strong on small objects

cols.title: One-stage
items: Boxes and classes predicted densely in one pass
Fast; the real-time default
Needs NMS afterwards

cols.title: Set prediction
items: A transformer predicts a fixed set of boxes
Bipartite matching to ground truth in training
No anchors, no NMS

slides.title: Inside a one-stage detector
slides.lede: From image to boxes in five stages. Post-processing is part of the model's behaviour, not an afterthought.

points.t: NMS deletes boxes overlapping the top one. In crowds that deletes real objects; Soft-NMS decays their scores instead.
The letterbox padding was not undone when mapping back to original coordinates.

slides.title: Anchors, or not
slides.lede: How a detector parameterises boxes decides what it can find easily.

cols.title: Anchor-based
items: Preset box priors at each location
The network predicts an offset from a prior
Priors that do not match object shapes cost recall

cols.title: Anchor-free
items: Regress distances to the box edges, or a centre heatmap
No anchor shapes to tune
Now the common design

points.t: Is anything here, separate from which class. The final score often multiplies the two.
Optimises the overlap that evaluation measures, and is scale-invariant — unlike L1 on coordinates.

slides.title: IoU, and the three places it appears
slides.lede: Intersection over union measures box overlap. It is used three times in a detector's life, each with its own threshold and meaning.

items.label: the measure
items.text: Area of overlap divided by area of union. 1 is a perfect match.

items.label: Anchor assignment
items.text: In training: which prior is responsible for which ground-truth box.

items.label: NMS
items.text: In post-processing: how much overlap makes two boxes duplicates.

items.label: Evaluation
items.text: In scoring: how much overlap counts as a correct detection.

slides.title: Reading mAP
slides.lede: Mean average precision is the standard score and is easy to misread.

items.label: same model, different numbers
items.text: COCO averages IoU 0.5 to 0.95; VOC uses 0.5 alone. Never compare them directly.

items.label: not your operating point
items.text: mAP averages over confidence thresholds. You deploy at one — choose it from the PR curve.

items.label: then averaged
items.text: A good mean can hide a class that fails. Read the per-class table.

slides.title: Why detectors fail
slides.lede: Match the symptom to its usual cause before retraining anything.

rows: Input resolution too low, or no shallow pyramid level for small scales
Confidence threshold too high, or anchor priors that do not fit the shapes
NMS threshold too aggressive — try Soft-NMS
Good on validation, poor on a new camera
Domain shift: new viewpoint, scale distribution, lighting
Inconsistent labels in the training data

chapters.hook: Labelling every pixel: which task, which architecture, and which number to trust.

slides.title: Three kinds of segmentation
slides.lede: They differ in whether they separate individual objects and whether they cover every pixel.

cols.title: Semantic
items: Every pixel gets a class
Two touching cars merge into one region
Cannot count objects

cols.title: Instance
items: A separate mask for each object
Countable things only
Traditionally ignores amorphous ‘stuff’ like sky or road

cols.title: Panoptic
items: Every pixel gets a class
Countable things also get an instance ID
The complete scene description

points.t: Segment when shape, area or boundary matters. A box is enough when you only need presence and position.

slides.title: Encoder, decoder and skips
slides.lede: Downsampling builds meaning but loses detail. The decoder has to restore resolution, and skip connections hand it the detail back.

visual.loop: U-Net skip connections carry each encoder level's high-resolution detail across to the decoder

points.t: A transposed convolution whose stride does not divide its kernel size. Resize, then convolve.
Parallel dilated convolutions at several rates, for multi-scale context without downsampling.

slides.title: Instance masks: Mask R-CNN and SAM
slides.lede: Instance segmentation usually starts from a detector and adds a mask per region.

points.t: Quantised RoI pooling misaligns features by up to a pixel — invisible for boxes, visible in masks.
SAM produces class-agnostic masks from a point, a box or a rough mask.

slides.title: Which number to trust
slides.lede: Segmentation metrics that look alike report very different things.

items.label: Dice = 2·IoU / (1 + IoU)
items.text: They rank models identically but report different numbers. Check which a paper used.

items.label: pixel accuracy vs mIoU
items.text: A few large classes dominate the pixel count. mIoU averages per class and refuses to hide failures.

items.label: the best threshold
items.text: Under class imbalance, sweep the binary threshold on validation.

items.label: Dice loss
items.text: Stays sensitive when the foreground is tiny. Often summed with cross-entropy.

slides.title: Segmentation in practice
slides.lede: Masks, large images and new sites each bring their own failure.

items.label: Augment masks with images
items.text: Apply the identical geometric transform, and resize masks with nearest-neighbour only.

items.label: Tile large images
items.text: Too big for memory? Tile with overlap, segment, and blend the overlaps to avoid seams.

items.label: Across sites
items.text: Scanners, cameras and protocols differ. Split and evaluate by site to see the generalisation gap.

chapters.hook: Images as sequences, images with text, and images from noise.

slides.title: An image as a sequence of patches
slides.lede: A vision transformer cuts the image into patches and treats them like words.

points.t: CNNs get locality and translation equivariance for free; ViTs must learn them — hence their appetite for data.
Fine-tuning at another size means interpolating the positional embeddings onto the new patch grid.

slides.title: Why resolution is expensive
slides.lede: One arithmetic fact explains most efficient-attention designs.

items.label: resolution to tokens
items.text: Doubling the image side quadruples the patch count.

items.label: tokens to cost
items.text: Every token attends to every other token.

items.label: together
items.text: Double the side length, pay sixteen times for attention.

slides.takeaway: Swin's answer: attend within local windows, shift the windows between layers, and merge patches into a hierarchy — cost grows linearly with image size.

slides.title: CLIP and zero-shot recognition
slides.lede: Train an image encoder and a text encoder so that matching pairs land close together. Classes become text you can change at inference.

nodes.label: Two encoders
nodes.sub: One for images, one for text

nodes.label: Contrastive training
nodes.sub: Pull true pairs together, push others apart

nodes.label: Zero-shot
nodes.sub: Embed class names; pick the nearest

points.h: A new class is a string
points.t: Open-vocabulary detection extends this: categories are named in text at inference, not fixed at training.
Weak on fine-grained or specialised domains far from web imagery, and sensitive to prompt wording.

slides.title: Learning without labels
slides.lede: Self-supervised pretraining learns strong features from unlabelled images, so a small labelled set goes much further.

cols.title: DINO
items: A student matches a teacher across different views of the same image
No labels anywhere
Features that cluster by object

cols.title: MAE
items: Hide most patches of the image
Reconstruct the missing pixels
Cheap: the encoder sees only visible patches

slides.takeaway: With a few thousand labelled images, fine-tune or freeze a pretrained backbone. Never train a ViT from scratch at that scale.

slides.title: Diffusion: images from noise
slides.lede: A diffusion model learns to remove noise. Generation runs that in reverse, from pure noise to an image, guided by a prompt.

points.t: Denoising a compressed latent is far cheaper than working at full pixel resolution.
A dial between prompt adherence and diversity.

chapters.hook: Motion, identity over time, and pipelines that keep up with the cameras.

slides.title: Tracking by detection
slides.lede: Detect objects in each frame, then decide which detection belongs to which existing track.

nodes.label: Predict
nodes.sub: Kalman filter: where each track should be

nodes.label: Associate
nodes.sub: Hungarian matching on a cost matrix

visual.loop: every frame; unmatched tracks coast briefly on prediction, then retire

points.t: Box overlap, and an appearance embedding when objects cross or disappear.
Frames are highly redundant: detect periodically and propagate cheaply in between.

slides.title: Identity is the hard part
slides.lede: Finding objects is detection's job. Keeping their identities straight over time is where trackers fail.

items.label: Identity switch
items.text: Two tracks swap IDs where paths cross. Appearance re-identification fixes it.

items.label: Re-ID embeddings
items.text: Trained so identity, not category, sets the distance. Survive occlusion and camera changes.

items.label: frame rate matters
items.text: At low frame rates objects move too far for IoU association and constant-velocity prediction.

items.label: Count on crossings
items.text: Count a track crossing a line with direction and hysteresis — not per-frame presence in a region.

slides.title: Scoring a tracker
slides.lede: Two standard metrics that answer different questions. A tracker can score well on one and badly on the other.

cols.title: MOTA
items: Misses, false positives and identity switches in one number
Dominated by detection quality
Barely notices a few ID switches

cols.title: IDF1
items: How long each object keeps the right ID
Isolates association quality
The one to read when identity matters

slides.title: Motion and optical flow
slides.lede: Optical flow estimates how each pixel moved between frames. It measures apparent motion, not true motion.

cols.title: Sparse
items: Tracks selected keypoints
Fast
Motion only where there are features

cols.title: Dense
items: A motion vector for every pixel
Costlier
Full motion field

points.t: Flow assumes a point keeps its brightness. Lighting changes, highlights and occlusion break it.
Object motion, camera motion and lighting change all look alike in the flow field.

slides.title: Time carries meaning
slides.lede: Some things cannot be read from a single frame. Sitting down and standing up look identical in a still.

cols.title: Single frame
items: Appearance only
Ambiguous for actions
Cannot tell direction or speed

cols.title: Temporal model
items: Change over time is the signal
Two-stream: appearance plus motion from flow
Or clip-level 3D or video-transformer models

slides.title: A multi-camera pipeline
slides.lede: At scale, video decoding and data movement often cost more than the model itself.

nodes.label: GPU decode
nodes.sub: CPU H.264 decode often costs more than inference

points.t: When processing falls behind, drop stale frames rather than let queues grow without bound — old frames are worthless.

chapters.hook: What your labels, splits and metrics can and cannot tell you.

slides.title: Labels set the ceiling
slides.lede: A model cannot be measured as more accurate than the labels it is scored against.

items.label: Inter-annotator agreement
items.text: The ceiling on measured performance. Where humans disagree, the ground truth is noise.

items.label: Guidelines
items.text: State the occlusion rule and how to treat depictions — posters, screens, reflections.

items.label: Confusion is often taxonomy
items.text: Two classes confused with each other often means an unclear class definition, not a weak model.

items.label: Pseudo-labels
items.text: Inherit the teacher's systematic errors — and random spot checks cannot see consistent errors.

slides.title: Split without leaking
slides.lede: If near-duplicate images land on both sides of a split, the test score measures memory, not generalisation.

cols.title: Random split
items: Adjacent video frames on both sides
Same patient or site in train and test
Inflated scores that collapse in deployment

cols.title: Grouped split
items: Split by video, patient, site or session
Near-duplicates removed across splits
Cross-validation by group on small data

slides.title: Choosing and reading the metric
slides.lede: Pick the curve that stays honest under imbalance, then pick the one point you will actually deploy at.

cols.title: ROC
items: False-positive rate divides by all negatives
A huge negative class makes it look excellent
Flatters imbalanced problems

cols.title: Precision–recall
items: Precision counts false positives against predictions
Shows the cost of each extra detection
The right curve for rare positives

points.t: 0.812 vs 0.807 mAP on 400 images is noise. Check variance across seeds before declaring a winner.
Shows which classes are confused with which — the first place to look after a headline number.

slides.title: Report the slices
slides.lede: An aggregate score can improve while the cases you care most about get worse.

items.label: Per class
items.text: Rare and safety-critical classes reported on their own.

items.label: Per capture condition
items.text: Night, rain, glare, each camera and site.

items.label: Regression suite
items.text: Known-hard cases that once failed, run on every change.

items.label: Benchmarks
items.text: Rank architectures. They do not predict your accuracy on your domain.

slides.title: When the world moves
slides.lede: Deployed data drifts away from the training data. Name the kind of shift before choosing a response.

head: Shift
What changes
Example
rows: The inputs; the task stays the same
A new camera, lighting or season — the common one
A defect becomes rarer after a process fix
The link between input and label
What counts as a defect is redefined

slides.takeaway: Vision models degrade silently. Monitor input statistics and prediction counts, and re-run the regression suite on fresh samples.

chapters.hook: Getting a trained model onto real hardware, fast, and keeping it honest there.

slides.title: From checkpoint to engine
slides.lede: Each conversion step can change the model's behaviour silently. Validate against the original after every one.

nodes.label: Validate again
nodes.sub: Accuracy on the tasks that matter

points.t: Control flow and computed shapes become constants in the exported graph. Test several input shapes.
A TensorRT engine is built for one GPU architecture. Rebuild for each target.

slides.title: Precision and what it costs
slides.lede: Lower precision is faster and smaller. Whether it is safe depends on what the output feeds.

cols.title: FP16
items: Floating point, with an exponent
No calibration needed
Usually safe

cols.title: INT8
items: Needs a calibration pass over representative data
Sets per-tensor scales
Faster still, riskier

slides.takeaway: INT8 often keeps classification accuracy while hurting detection mAP: only the argmax matters for a class, but box coordinates feed straight into IoU. Keep sensitive layers at higher precision.

slides.title: Compression that actually speeds things up
slides.lede: Fewer parameters does not automatically mean faster inference. The hardware has to be able to use the savings.

cols.title: Pruning
items: Remove weights or channels, then fine-tune to recover
Structured pruning — whole channels — gives real speedups
Scattered zeros often do not, on dense hardware

cols.title: Distillation
items: A small student learns a large teacher's soft outputs
The soft outputs carry more than hard labels
A genuinely smaller, faster architecture

slides.title: Where the frame time goes
slides.lede: A model benchmarked alone at 28 FPS can run at 9 FPS in the application. The model is only one stage of the loop.

points.t: Batching raises frames per second and raises each frame's wait. One live camera cannot batch without adding the latency it hoped to avoid.
Decode, preprocess and infer without host round trips; copies often cost more than the model.

slides.title: Monitoring without labels
slides.lede: In the field there is no ground truth. Vision models fail silently, so watch what you can measure.

items.label: Preprocessing parity
items.text: Training and serving must resize, pad, normalise and order channels identically.

items.label: Input statistics
items.text: Brightness, contrast, sharpness — a dirty lens or a new camera shows up here first.

items.label: Output statistics
items.text: Detections per frame and confidence distributions. A sudden change is a signal.

items.label: Validate every build
items.text: Compare the exported or quantised model with the original on fixed inputs.
